title: Omnichannel Retail Trends for CPG Brands
summary: Omnichannel retail trends for CPG: how pickup, delivery, and marketplace changed the shelf, and how to measure a category that spans online and store.
body_markdown:
Omnichannel retail trends get discussed as a technology story and land on a brand as a measurement problem. Most grocery ecommerce is fulfilled from the same store shelf that serves walk-in shoppers, which means a growing share of your volume is bought by someone who never saw your package, chosen from a screen where search rank replaces shelf position.


That single fact changes more for a CPG brand than any of the channel forecasts, and most syndicated measurement was built before it was true.


One definition first, because the omnichannel shopper gets described as a separate audience and is not one. The omnichannel shopper is a single household using more than one fulfillment mode at the same retailer across a period: in store this week, pickup the next, delivery when the week goes sideways. Mode belongs to the trip rather than to the person, so an ecommerce persona built alongside an in-store persona usually describes the same household twice. Following that household across modes takes loyalty-linked or panel data, because scan data carries transactions and not people, which is a good argument for spending the effort on what the trip looks like instead of on who the shopper is.


## Key takeaways


- Search rank is the new shelf position for the online-fulfilled share of your volume, and it is a different competition.
- Substitution is a real, measurable loss unique to online. Out of stock becomes a competitor's sale rather than a deferred one.
- Product content is now merchandising. Title, images, and attributes determine whether you appear at all.
- Store-fulfilled online orders sit inside store POS, so a channel-split read is harder than it looks.


## The omnichannel retail trends that changed the shelf


In store Online Consequence


Shelf position and eye level Search rank and category page position A new competition your field team cannot influence.


Package design and claims Thumbnail, title, and attribute filters Content quality is merchandising, not marketing collateral.


Shopper sees an out of stock and may wait A substitute is offered automatically Out of stock converts directly to a competitor trial.


Impulse and adjacency Reorder lists and past purchases Habit is reinforced. Trial gets harder for a challenger.


Price comparison across the fixture Price sorting and unit-price display Price transparency is higher, so index position matters more.


The fourth row is the one that most changes competitive dynamics. A reorder list is the strongest form of habit a brand can hold, and it makes an established item substantially harder to displace. For an incumbent that is a moat; for a challenger it means trial has to be bought somewhere other than the shelf.


## The measurement problem


Store-fulfilled ecommerce rings through the store's POS. So the units are in your store-level data, attributed to a physical store, with no flag saying a shopper never entered it.


Three consequences follow. Store-level velocity now blends two different shopping behaviors. A store with a large pickup operation looks like a high-velocity store when it is partly a fulfillment center. And a field visit to check the shelf tells you nothing about the online share of that store's volume.


The fix is partial and worth doing anyway: get channel-split reporting from retailers that provide it, treat pure-play and marketplace volume separately, and flag your highest-pickup stores so their velocity is read in context rather than as a merchandising success.


## What to measure that you probably do not


- Search rank for your top ten category terms at each major retailer, tracked weekly. This is the online equivalent of a shelf audit and almost nobody runs it.
- Content completeness: title, image count, attribute fields, and description against the retailer's own spec. Incomplete content removes you from filtered results entirely.
- Online out-of-stock rate, which behaves differently from in-store because it is visible instantly and triggers a substitution.
- Ratings and review counts, which function as a conversion driver in a way they never did on a physical shelf.


A worked example: a brand found its 16 oz item ranked 14th for its main category term at one retailer, below three items with lower velocity. The cause was two missing attribute fields that excluded it from the two most-used filters. Fixing the content took a week and moved the item to 6th. No pricing, promotion, or distribution change was involved, and no existing report would have surfaced the problem.


One organizational consequence worth naming, because it decides whether any of this gets fixed. Online product content is usually owned by an ecommerce or marketing team, while shelf performance is owned by sales. When an item is missing from a retail search filter, the person who can see the sales impact and the person who can edit the attribute field are in different functions with different priorities, and the fix waits. Brands that assign one owner for how the item appears at each retailer, on shelf and on screen, resolve these in days instead of quarters.


The broader point about omnichannel retail trends is that almost none of the required work is new technology. It is checking that your items are findable, complete, in stock, and correctly priced on a second shelf you cannot walk. That is the same job the field team has always done, performed against a different surface, and most brands have not assigned it to anyone.


## How Scout fits


Scout reads store-level POS and can hold a channel dimension where the retailer supplies one, so a high-pickup store is not silently read as a merchandising win. Where the split is unavailable, keeping distribution, velocity, and price together at least makes the anomaly visible rather than invisible, which is the first requirement for asking the retailer a specific question.


Related:[attribute tagging](https://www.cpgscout.ai/glossary/attribute-tagging) and[POS data](https://www.cpgscout.ai/blog/pos-data) .


## Frequently asked questions


What does omnichannel mean for a CPG brand specifically?That a growing share of your volume is selected on a screen rather than at a shelf, usually fulfilled from the same store. Search rank replaces shelf position, product content replaces package design as the merchandising lever, and out of stock converts to a competitor's sale through automatic substitution.


Can I separate online from in-store sales?Only partly. Store-fulfilled ecommerce rings through store POS with no flag. Some retailers provide channel-split reporting; otherwise treat pure-play and marketplace separately and identify your highest-pickup stores so their velocity is read in context.


Why does product content matter so much?Attribute fields drive filtered search results. Missing fields can exclude an item from the filters shoppers actually use, which removes it from consideration entirely regardless of price, distribution, or demand.


Is online out of stock worse than in store?Generally yes, because the platform offers a substitute immediately. In store a shopper may wait or come back; online the out of stock converts directly into trial for a competitor.
